work.author: Balai of Balsh
work.title: On Bishop Acacius
work.edition: Machine translation (gpt-6.1-sol, Patristica, 2026-10-28) of: Julian Joseph Overbeck S. Ephraemi Syri, Rabulae episcopi Edesseni, Balaei aliorumque Oper; TEI by J. E. Walters, Digital Syriac Corpus (syriaccorpus.org 504)

paragraphs.text: Hymns of Mar Balai, spoken by him about the blessed Mar Acacius, the bishop. To the tune of “O my Lord, in your gardens.”
Our father, on your feast day show me kindness. Offer a petition to your Lord, that he may grant me the ability to tell of your triumph.
If you do not neglect me, your Lord will not withhold. He opens and gives to me, not because I am worthy, but because you have been found worthy.
All the beautiful qualities that deserve praise were gathered in your life. Your tongue was diligent and sowed purity.
Your gaze raised barriers among the young men, and your eye planted a warning in the boys, so that they would acquire chastity.
Whoever heard your words believed; otherwise, he looked at your conduct and was convinced. Your labor was your witness.
You cultivated the love of God through deeds, and after acquiring it, you shared it through words, so that your companions might increase.
Your heart rejoiced in those who were upright, and your voice strengthened those who were weak, so that they might walk with the upright.
You counseled whoever possessed it not to lose it. Whoever lacked it heard from you and toiled and labored to possess it.
The rich man heard from you that his treasure should be his portion [?], and that he should not doze and sleep, lest robbers come with bloodshed and remorse.
You extended a hand so that those who had fallen might rise. With your words you supported whoever was standing, so that he would not fall and die.
You stripped off the love of possessions, O athlete. In the contest you yourself labored alone and triumphed because you were unencumbered.
You traveled fearlessly among the [?] of robbers, for you yourself passed through the world alone, carrying love instead of wealth.
You placed the merchandise you had carried before everyone: a consolation for you and an example for another, so that he might labor as you did.
The evil one [?] devised his schemes, but his tricks were blunted against you. Though you wore a body, no arrow pierced you, for fasting was your armor.
Your body did not deceive you; the evil one did not overpower you. Your course was not checked, for it was not someone weaker than you who rose against you.
You counseled your soul to labor and practiced self-denial. The body that helped it chose its counsel, for the benefit was shared.
The body abandoned its habits and drew close to the soul. When the soul saw that it had joined it, it fed the body its own bread: fasting and prayer.
Once your body became accustomed to the habits of your spirit, and its food became pleasant to it, it changed and became spiritual, so that it would not lose its bread.
Good deeds fashioned wings for the body, so that it might fly with the soul and reach that light of Eden.
The second hymn. To the same tune.
You were one person, O our aged father, yet virtues grew within you, each one of which surpassed its companions.
Whoever saw you was astonished and amazed that a single human being contained the likenesses of so many righteous people.
Your pure virginity was planted in your body. Its beauty remained in you, for its fruit dwelt in you; with its blessings it enriched you.
It placed its light within you, for it found you to be its dwelling. Though it was hidden, its rays shone out from you, so that you in turn might be adorned by it.
Your will also drove desire out of your body, lest filth soil and blacken the dignity of the soul, its mistress.
Desire was no dishonorable guest in your body. Therefore your chaste virginity was not angered; she spent all her years with you.
Her companions shone in keeping with her purity: fasting and almsgiving helped her, in your [?] for purity.
The blessing you gave Elijah endures. You did not wrong the dwelling where she found rest; her gain was on high.

Your strength, mighty man, overcame hardships within you. Your will cut your body's bonds with your sword, your purity. All these beauties we have mentioned are manifest and rest within your body, though there are others we have left unmentioned.
Your youth preserved the beauty of your childhood. Pure from the womb and radiant to the grave, you are chosen for the resurrection.
Your birth was pure, and your departure radiant. Death took you as its entrusted charge, just as you were as a child, to the grave without debts.
And since the grave cannot contain your purity, it gives birth to you and hands you over to the bosom of the kingdom, with your beauty still within you.
Your struggle was prolonged, and your victory grew rich. The older it grew, the stronger it became, conquering and triumphing.
A course easy for a young man is hard for an old man. Yet your old age labored, and young men marveled at it. They ran but did not get ahead of you.
Your foot was eager to travel the road. Your purity cleared the path of stones so that you could walk without fear.
Your body grew weak, but your labor grew stronger. Your flesh diminished, but your running increased, for your Lord was your strength.
[?] made your body waste away, for blows choked it. Your body remained a sign that the soul was awake within it.
Your body's activities did not oppress your soul, for purity drove away the habits of the flesh so that your spirit might live.
Your heel rested on the serpent's head, lest your thought turn back and sting your very self, and you die by your own doing.
Your Lord, whom you loved, strengthened your mind so that within it you could seize and kill contemptible thoughts, the offspring of the body.
All desires fell asleep within you and became silent. They became dead women whose months had come to term, but whose infants never came forth.
You gave birth to truth and killed injustice. Your will was a sword that slaughtered evil things and brought good things to life.
You mastered your body and subdued the rebel. No one can defeat someone who has escaped his own body. You conquered everything by conquering it.
Zealous Phinehas, whose strength was his purity, conquered his one body and killed two unclean people whose wickedness [?] before him.
Your zeal also counseled you, blessed one, to constrain your body and obey your soul so that both might live.
The third. To the same tune.
Like a craftsman, you forged armor and clothed people's bodies in it without charge, so that they might conquer as you did.
In time of battle you went out in front. When there was peace, you worked on armor to clothe others.
You taught what you practiced, and you practiced the very thing your Lord had commanded should be done.
Your mouth spoke, and your labor bore witness that your lap was full of the fruits of your teaching. Deeds and labors.
The things in your mouth were also in your body. Your deeds confirmed the word of your [?]. In words and actions.
You displayed an example in yourself, as it is written, for you first did what you said.
What you did was the very thing your mouth laid down as a law for everyone. And to the ear that heard you, the eye testified that your teaching was embodied in you.
Your teaching delighted the listener, our father, for the discourse of your tongue was spread over your image, and the eyes bore witness.
The listeners did not accuse you even in their thoughts, for the word of your tongue was fixed in your body in the beauty of your salvation.
Ears and eyes heard and saw the truth, for while the ear listened, behold, the eye delighted—in hearing and in sight.
You taught well because you practiced what you taught. Your words were accepted because of your labors, for your Lord gave help through you.
Who could bear the fruits of your teaching? You yourself bore the weight that your tongue prescribed and imposed.
Your tree was one, and its fruits were many, for in one person were countless virtues spread over you.
The eyes [?] a well-ordered sight, and the ear fed on the sound of purity that your mouth sang.
Every day the fruits of your branches are picked, and others are quickly born in their place, being born every day.
Your trust was your Lord, who planted you beside living waters, and every day you brought forth the fruit of uprightness.
The apostle wrote the book of the Spirit, and you received it. He marveled at you because you [?] it—not because you read it, but because you kept it.
Through his commandments he marked out varied paths for you, and you became a traveler equal to the roads that the guide showed.
Your free will passed through the furnace of his afflictions. You looked at his sufferings and rejoiced in your own, because your labor resembled his.

At sea and on the seas you preached, and he was tossed about. And behold, you too are at sea and in the four quarters. Your labor was in the church. You had clothed yourself in the concern of which the apostle wrote, and you labored everywhere for the churches, to give your Lord rest.
With your peace you broke through the wall of strife, and with love you humbled the heights of anger, so that the church might be at peace.
You considered a heavy burden light, for you increased your labor, remembering the reward appointed for your toil.
I offered a prayer and approached your story: may my tongue bear fruit through you, for my mind has loved you. May I please your Lord through you.
Of four. Its melody.
I return to your story so that I may be helped by you, so that I may cherish your love, which does not send away empty-handed the mind that meditates on it.
Every day I sought to fix my gaze on you, so that my mind might rejoice in you, my prayer might delight in you, and my love might pay you homage.
My thought hovered over you, and my tongue constrained it, for what is visible cannot express [?] the hidden things that the mind conceives.
Whoever wished to marvel at you came and saw: your dwelling belonged to the poor, and your hand belonged to the generous. While still a child, you conceived.
Every day you sowed, and your storehouse grew. Your generous hand could not exhaust your wealth, for through your hand your Lord was giving.
Your dwelling was poor, but your hand was rich, for every day it was full of nourishment for the hungry—the fruits of almsgiving.
Our Lord sustained the practice of your hand, so that your practice might endure, for you had made the Giver’s mercies your practice.
The rooms of your dwelling were empty and bare, but the hollows of your fingers were full and overflowing with satisfaction for the hungry.
Your hand was outdone, for your treasury grew. So that you might give, [?], and your provider strengthened you, for your Lord is greater than you.
Because you carried out his commandments, he carried out your wishes. You called him and he answered you, and he heaped up treasures so that your hand might be praised.
You received from your Lord a reward for what you had done. He doubled it and added more for you, because you taught others to see and imitate.
Like someone eager, you approached fasting with love. You dwelt in a skin, treating your belly with contempt. Your delight was in Eden.
You did not eat greedily, nor did you fast boastfully. You apportioned weights to match the burdens, and these contributed to your crown.
Even when you ate, you were serving fasting, for the food of your pure table was fasting. It was the body that you were sustaining,
so that the body would not grow weak and cease running. You subdued it without letting the soul flee from within it while it was still making its journey.
No [?] faster passed you, old man. The weak caught up with you, and you slowed your fasting to match those walking.
Your fasting did not boast over anyone who was weak, nor did your mouth scold anyone who ate, so that you might become all things to everyone.
We see a marvel in you; let us praise your discernment. When you ate, it was fasting, and when you fasted, it was food. The one who did both was the same.
For you ate so that you would not become depleted, and you also fasted so that you would not stumble. Your eating was a help, and your fasting was a benefit. May your example endure among us.
You fulfilled what is written and did not eat alone. And therefore you fasted, so that you might become all things to everyone and help those reclining at table.
Your table bestowed an inheritance, as your exposition did, for your holy mouth praised radiantly and ate purely.
It spoke of hidden things and ate pure things. It expounded fasting and restrained its lips, so that its word might be fulfilled in itself.
Your fasting helped us, and your table enriched us. The ear rejoiced in you, and you restrained the belly within you. You desired self-denial.
You stood as an example to everyone you taught, so that the apostle who wrote might rejoice that you had fulfilled his words. For I saw him in your own person.
In church was your radiance; in the marketplace, your modesty. Your heart carried the church wherever your holy body stayed.
The flock that loved you accompanied you everywhere, to benefit from your voice and to graze, at the sight of you, on examples drawn from your body.
The fifth. To the same tune.
From now on I will glory, for my contest is complete. Listen to me, my Savior, for I have gained confidence, since I have not disobeyed your command.
At the time of parting, boasting is fitting, for there is no assurance until death, because life is full of deceit.
All the days of my life I walked in fear; because of the course I was running, I went along anxiously. Now fear has ceased.
Death is the seal that safeguards one's trading; it receives the race and hands over the deposit to everyone according to his labor.
Bodies decay, but labors are preserved. Bodies are raised, and deeds come forward, and from them come rewards.
The body lies silent in the dust for a whole span of time. Although its movements have ceased, its labors are not forgotten, for the one who records them is wise.
We acted and forgot, but you preserved what was ours. At the resurrection, the deeds we performed will be read aloud in our hearing.
For the one who has forgotten, his good deeds will spring up before his eyes. Happy is he when he sees that the number of his evil deeds does not exceed his good deeds.
In the world I was afraid to recount my labors to you, because the evil one hid traps under pretexts. I escaped his snares.
I stood at your door by night and by day, for I had learned that you do not send those who knock away empty-handed if they are patient.
My life reached a hundred years in your service, and on the last day I labored as on the first, to please you all the more.
I bequeathed zeal to my children as a treasure, so that they might acquire courses of conduct that bring honor on the day of death.
I listened to you, Savior, and kept your commandment. Now I ask for the fulfillment of your words to the righteous who followed you.
Every day Satan changed his attacks. With the shield of my faith I deflected his arrows and shattered his victory.
My desire made no breaches in my armor, and there was no place for [?] in the furnace. Your remembrance forged it for me.
The evil one sat and laid snares for me, but he did not catch me. He saw me and was grieved that he had not put a single ugly blemish on your worker.
I passed among his schemes, and his snares did not entangle me. I stood firm in his battles and kept my limbs from the scratch of his arrow.
His deceit did not catch me, and his sword did not pierce me. I trod among his traps and passed among his arrows, and I came out victorious.
You have joy at my death because I kept myself pure, while my enemy mourns because his deceit did not condemn me and his arrow did not harm me.
My joy traveled with me, for my death is a joy to you. Because my adversary is distressed, my mind rejoices greatly, for I escaped and he did not seize me.
You left me with the evil one to fight, and I did not diminish your glory, for your servant was not defeated by the hater of your truth.
With your help, my Savior, I held off his assault. Every day he fought, and every day he was put to shame. With your weapons I was victorious.
He did not defeat me in his battles, because your grace was with me. He turned to enticing me, but I, who had experienced him, despised his pleasures.
I rejected his wine because I remembered your vinegar. I scorned delicacies because I remembered the bitter things his servants offered you.

I crucified my life for you as I pondered your cross, and I stretched out my hands to you, because I saw on the wood yours stretched out. I heard of the mockery you endured and despised honor. I remembered the spitting you endured and pressed myself to bear and endure.
Through your tunic, which they stripped off, you despised the clothing that you had honored, to your humiliation, in my lowly garment. Cover me with your glory.
